Campaign Concept FrameworkLast edit Aug 31

How a month of campaigns gets built

The calendar is a commercial plan before it's an email plan, so it gets built with the brand. From there the month splits into two tracks, because promo and content do different jobs, and blending them is how a brand ends up with a calendar that's just discounts with a story attached.

Track 1 · Promo, on the commercial actions

  • Headline-driven, no header image, offer carried by typography
  • Founder's letter, copy only
  • Launch day, one clear CTA
  • Back in stock
  • Mystery offer
  • Your favourites are on sale

Context is what changes them: subscriber exclusive, VIP early access, final hours, extended.

Track 2 · Content, two to four a week, no commercial ask

Educational
Authority + objection removal

  • FAQs and how it's made
  • The mistake most customers make
  • Using it in a daily routine
  • The science behind it
  • One benefit, explained
  • Step-by-step guide

Social proof
Specificity + transformation

  • A single testimonial line
  • Before and after
  • Customer of the month
  • Your words, not ours
  • Rated 4.9, here's why
  • Best rated by a group

Product
Highlight & collection

  • Bestsellers, new reason each time
  • One feature → one benefit
  • Seasonal top five
  • A combination that works
  • Comparison vs the alternative

One angle per email, one message per email. If it's saying three things it says nothing, and the tell is the subject line. When I can't write it in six words, the email has more than one idea in it and it gets split.

Flow Architecture PlaybookLast edit Sep 24

Build order, and why it's that order

Flows have a build order, not a menu, in falling order of leverage. Pre-purchase brings the first order. Post-purchase is where LTV actually gets built.

  • Trigger first: exclude test and staff emails, wholesale, fraud and POS orders, and set the minimum order and re-entry rules. The right email to the wrong person costs deliverability, not just the sale.
  • Pop-up: it grows the list every other flow depends on, and site and browse abandon only fire for identified profiles.
  • Welcome: one email a day, no gaps. 3, 5 or 8 emails (5 by default), at least one in plain text.
  • Site, browse, cart and checkout abandon: the deepest signal wins, so each flow exits when the person moves further down. Dynamic product block on top, copy that assumes the sale in tone, never in fact.
  • Post-purchase: relationship before sale. Feel good about the purchase, learn the product, and only then the repurchase nudge, timed against delivery.
  • Subscription cycle: pre-renewal, failed payment and cancel save, each with its own trigger. Usually the highest-margin flow in the account.
  • Winback and sunset: winback at around 3x the repurchase time, with store credit that has a face value and an expiry date. Sunset at 120 days without an open, protecting every other flow.

The playbook is the starting point, not the answer. The real repurchase window, how hard the abandonment flows can push, whether a list will take an email a day... all of it comes out of the brand's own data.

Campaigns

Written and shipped by me, in-house and on freelance. Screenshots from my own inbox, so this is what the subscriber saw. Copy is Portuguese; the teardown is mine.

InsiderWinback
Scroll for the full email

“Let's see if you're an Insider” · anti-sweat undershirts.

It doesn't open with an offer. A lapsed buyer in apparel didn't leave over price, they forgot the product solved something, so the email re-tells the founding problem.

Ratings and the fabric spec carry the objection work, and the referral offer sits at the very bottom, after the value rather than in front of it.

Old SillerProduct launch
Scroll for the full email

“NEW: St. Michael pendant” · silver jewellery.

The product is a religious medal, so the email leads with the painting and the meaning before it shows the object. You buy the story first.

A spec block then clears the buying questions in one screen, and a spend threshold adds a numbered piece, which lifts basket size without discounting anything.

EscultorLaunch anticipation
Scroll for the full email

“The biggest offer in our history is coming” · menswear.

This one sells the list, not the product. No prices, no products, one CTA repeated: join the waitlist.

Three reasons, all access rather than money. And it says plainly that this is not a clearance, which protects the brand while still promising the discount.

MidastimePrice drop
Scroll for the full email

“Last units, from R$79.90” · shapewear.

Product cards with the maths already done: was, you save, total. Nobody should have to calculate a discount to decide.

Review counts sit above the price, so proof arrives before the number, and the coupon stacks visibly on top of the drop.
